extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, peer-reviewers, systematic reviewers, research funders and policymakers concerned with publication bias in biomedical research
extracted.subtask_short: preventing publication bias in biomedical research
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for identifying sources of publication bias and for policies/practices (peer review, registration, electronic publishing, conflict disclosure, reporting standards) that may prevent or reduce biased dissemination of biomedical research findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance decisions should not be based on study results
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance of manuscripts for publication by journal editors should not be determined by the direction or strength of study results; acceptance rates should not differ significantly between studies with positive/significant results and those with null/negative results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence from cohort studies and a pooled odds ratio (OR 1.06; 95% CI: 0.80 to 1.39) suggested no significant association between acceptance and direction/strength of findings in the studies reviewed. Nevertheless, some cohorts showed tendencies (e.g. JAMA tendency p=0.07; subgroup analyses with differing acceptance by result), indicating biased selection by investigators and possibly editors cannot be completely ruled out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigators should write up and submit all studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigators' failure to write up and submit completed studies (especially negative or non-significant studies) is a major source of publication bias and should be addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because acceptance at journals was not consistently determined by results, publication bias may largely be due to biased selection of studies to submit; investigators may abandon small or negative studies because they are cheap/easy to drop or because of anticipated rejection or sponsor/editor pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors should incorporate readers' perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal editorial policy should reflect readers' preferences and consider relevance to clinical practice; editors should find ways to incorporate readers’ perspectives into peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A survey of readers showed dissatisfaction with lack of manuscripts relevant to practice. Editors balancing readers' curiosity for novelty versus clinicians' preference for established treatments may affect what is published; studying the effect of incorporating readers' perspectives is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require disclosure of competing interests/conflict of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors (and ideally peer-reviewers and editors) should disclose financial and other competing interests to reduce bias due to research funding and commercial interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most journals report author COI policies (93% in one survey) and 77% collect COI information, but only 57% publish author disclosures; publishing COIs for peer-reviewers (3%) and editors (12%) is rare. Disclosure is important but may be insufficient alone to prevent bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish conflict of interest disclosures (authors, reviewers, editors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should not only collect conflict of interest information but publish disclosures for authors, and where appropriate for peer-reviewers and editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey data show only a minority publish such disclosures (57% publish author disclosures; 3% publish reviewer disclosures; 12% publish editor disclosures). Publishing disclosures increases transparency and highlights relationships with industry that may influence reporting or conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware disclosure can exacerbate bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of conflicts of interest may have counterintuitive effects (e.g. subconsciously absolving authors) and is insufficient by itself to prevent biased interpretation or reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A study by Cain et al. showed disclosure may exacerbate bias. While disclosure appears transparent, it can fail to prevent bias; additional measures are necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prospective registration of trials and protocols
rubrics_metrics.description: Prospective registration of clinical trials (and ideally other study types) at inception should be promoted or required as a condition for publication to reduce selective reporting and non-publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retrospective registration/amnesties largely failed; Lancet began assessing and registering selected protocols in 1997, but few protocols were accepted. Prospective registration makes the existence and pre-stated outcomes transparent and can be a precondition for journal consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepublication and publication of research protocols
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish research protocols prior to study completion so discrepancies between protocol and final report are transparent and outcome reporting bias can be detected/prevented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electronic publication of protocols (e.g. Cochrane systematic review protocols are peer reviewed and published before review completion) allows feedback on methodology and prevents duplication; publication of protocols allows outcome reporting transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic publishing and archiving to reduce space-related bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Use electronic publication and archiving (no space limits) to allow publication of negative/null studies, replication studies, and fuller methods/results to reduce bias based on novelty or space constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages include rapid publication, no length/number limits, interconnected articles and cost-effective archiving. Electronic journals can publish supplementary materials and full datasets; examples include BMJ's ELPS and online BioMed models. Direct empirical evidence for impact is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish peer-review reports and authors' responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish peer-review reports, initial submitted versions and authors' responses alongside accepted papers to increase transparency of the review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some online journals publish initial versions with reviewer comments and author replies; peer review transparency could make editorial decisions and reporting practices more accountable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt models that separate detailed methods/data from concise narrative (ELPS/Trial Bank)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use publication models (e.g. 'electronic long–paper short' or Trial Bank Model) that combine concise printed narratives with extensive online supplementary data to fulfill both 'medical recorder' and 'medical newspaper' functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These models let journals serve as both a record (detailed data) and news (concise, readable summaries), aiding publication of full information even when readers prefer shorter pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journals should consider accepting manuscripts based mainly on protocols
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals could commit to accept manuscripts for publication mainly on the basis of pre-submitted and assessed research protocols to ensure main outcomes are published irrespective of results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Lancet's initiative in 1997 to assess and register selected trial protocols and provide a commitment to peer review of main findings is an example; however, limited uptake shows practical challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support and use reporting guidelines to improve transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Endorse and apply established reporting guidelines (CONSORT, STARD, QUOROM/PRISMA, STROBE) and networks (EQUATOR) to ensure transparent and complete reporting of studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These guidelines aim to prevent incomplete and biased reporting for specific study designs. Further empirical evidence is required to quantify their impact on reporting bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review quality interventions (blinding and checklists) should be evaluated
rubrics_metrics.description: Interventions to improve peer review quality such as blinding reviewers to author identity and using submission checklists may influence review quality but evidence is mixed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A systematic review identified nine RCTs of blinding with mixed results (five no effect, four showed effect but with practical blinding difficulties); two studies on submission checklists gave mixed findings. Peer review remains important but evidence for specific improvements is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish journals dedicated to negative results and replication
rubrics_metrics.description: Support journals or outlets that explicitly publish negative or null findings and replication studies to reduce selective publication of positive results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Journal of Negative Results in Biomedicine (open access) launched in 2002; indexed and had published 60 articles by Aug 2008. Such venues improve retrievability of negative results for systematic reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit contractual sponsor powers over publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Research contracts should limit sponsors' contractual rights to delete or delay publication and restrict sponsor control over data/publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An editorial noted many university–industry agreements allowed sponsor deletion (35%), delay (53%), or both (30%). Limiting such rights helps prevent suppression of unfavorable results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure access to raw data and independent analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Facilitate independent access to raw trial data and independent analysis to detect selective reporting or misrepresentation by sponsors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case studies (e.g. Vioxx litigation, suppressed analyses) show that independent access and analysis have revealed discrepant and clinically important findings not reported in publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise industry sponsorship can be associated with pro-industry conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Be alert that industry sponsorship is statistically associated with more favorable study conclusions and/or lower transparency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic reviews found pooled ORs showing industry-sponsored studies more likely to reach pro-industry conclusions (Bekelman pooled OR 3.60; Lexchin pooled OR 4.05); industry-supported meta-analyses were less transparent and had more favourable conclusions than Cochrane reviews in comparative studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small sample size as a risk factor for publication bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies with small sample sizes have greater variability in results and present a wider range of outcomes from which selective publication can occur, increasing risk of publication bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simulations show substantial bias when only significant results are published and sample sizes are small; bias reduces when many large-scale trials exist. Small trials may be abandoned or not submitted when negative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small or moderate true effect sizes increase publication bias risk
rubrics_metrics.description: True effects that are small or moderate (as opposed to zero or large) are more prone to biased estimation due to selective publication of significant findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simulations demonstrated that the difference between true and biased effect estimates is largest when the true effect is small or moderate. Many clinical trials target small/moderate but clinically important effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study design and other quality characteristics influence susceptibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain study types (non-randomised, single-centre, phase I/II trials, and diagnostic test studies) may be more susceptible to publication bias than randomised, multicentre, phase III trials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These designs may be easier to abandon or may lack clear records of attempted evaluations (diagnostic accuracy), making them at higher risk for selective non-publication; assessment of how easy abandonment would be is useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic journals should consider the pay-to-publish model effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that open access electronic journals may charge authors a fee to publish and the impact of pay-to-publish models on publication bias and study quality is unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While electronic open access can increase publication of negative results, the author-fee model's effects on bias and quality require further study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate and document case studies of suppression and selective reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematically identify and summarise case studies where industry or other parties suppressed or selectively reported research findings to provide direct evidence of suppression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appendix 16 summarises high-profile cases (legal actions, suppression of trial results, blocked meta-analyses) that illustrate mechanisms of commercial suppression and selective reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use registration/publication initiatives but monitor uptake and enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement registration and protocol-publication initiatives but monitor their uptake and impact, as limited registration (e.g., Lancet protocol registry) has had low absolute numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lancet accepted ~75 protocols by 2007; such measures are promising but not yet widely adopted — limited uptake reduces their preventive potential unless more broadly enforced.
